memory_candidates.content: When a hand-rolled validator needs the deployed .claude/scripts/ tree for a sub-check (e.g. shelling out to another script that requires deploy-root-guard.sh), design the validator itself to be argument-relative (no PROJECT_ROOT dependency) so it can still be unit-tested directly from the source store; only the sub-check that genuinely needs the deployed tree (verify-deploy.sh's Gate 10 invoking the deployed validate-state.sh) needs the deploy step. This avoids forcing every consumer through deploy-headless.sh just to exercise the validator's core logic.

A verification-bullet grep asserting 'X returns zero hits' in a plan can be defeated by your OWN explanatory prose about X (e.g. a removal note naming the deleted values, or a comment explaining why a forbidden tool isn't used) -- the grep doesn't distinguish prose-about-X from live-X. When documenting a removal/prohibition, paraphrase the forbidden token instead of naming it literally (e.g. 'an in-progress marker and its completion counterpart' instead of the literal deleted status values, or 'a runtime JSON-Schema library' instead of naming the specific library) so the literal grep genuinely returns zero hits rather than being satisfied only in spirit.

index-entries.json's line_count field drifts silently whenever an edited file's line count changes, and check-extension-docs.sh's Rule R (or the standalone generate-context-line-counts.sh --check) is the only thing that catches it. Any implementation phase that edits a file already registered in index-entries.json should re-run generate-context-line-counts.sh --check (or manually diff wc -l against the declared line_count) before closing the phase, not just at final verification -- the drift is easy to introduce silently across multiple edits to the same file within one phase.
